summary: Jeremiah 28 (17 verses) continues the story of judgment. Starting with 'That same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows judgment lived out in jerusalem falling. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: That same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was of Gibeon, spoke to me in Yahweh’s hous
As for the prophet who prophesies of peace, when the word of the prophet happens, then the prophet will be known, that Yahweh has truly sent him.”
So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.

questions.question: What is happening in Jeremiah 28?
questions.answer: In 17 verses, this chapter jeremiah 28 (17 verses) continues the story of judgment. starting with 'that same year, in the beginning of the reign of zedekiah king of judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, hananiah the son of azzur, the prophet, who was', it moves through themes of judgment, new covenant and calls readers toward tears. The setting is jerusalem falling, written to judah before exile. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Jeremiah and why 28 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally jeremiah, addressed to judah before exile around ~600 bc. This chapter fits the book's purpose as prophetic laments — its themes of judgment, new covenant build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'prophet' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Messenger speaking for God. In this chapter, it appears in context of judgment. For a first-time reader: think of it as messenger speaking for god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through judgment and new covenant, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 1 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'That same year, in the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, Hananiah the son of Azzur, the prophet, who was of Gibeon, spoke to...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about judgment. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
